absent: Numeric values and full transition rules for slab_state stages beyond the FULL versus early distinction and the UP mark.
Complete layouts of kmem_cache, slab, kmalloc_info, saved_alias, sheaf and barn structures and their size calculations.
Locking rules for the global slab cache list and per-node per-CPU sheaf state outside the shown mutex regions.
Sysctl handler behavior, trace event payloads and memory-policy constraint evaluation for OOM victim selection.
Population of the NUMA distance table, memory block tables and emulated topology command line syntax.
Error paths for sysfs and debugfs creation failures beyond the alias link case.
Exact shift bounds and index mapping details for all general allocation sizes.

findings.text: Alias registration for slab caches. After full initialization it clears any stale link and links the supplied cache under the requested name in the slab hierarchy. Earlier in boot it queues the cache and name on a pending list for later materialization and reports allocation failure.

Alias identifier construction for mergeable caches. The name begins with a colon, appends one letter per set flag in the order lowercase d for DMA, uppercase D for DMA32, lowercase a for reclaim accounting, uppercase F for consistency checks and uppercase A for general accounting, adds a separator dash when any letter was emitted, then appends object size as zero padded decimal width 7. Allocation failure and length overflow yield error pointers.

Per-cache debug filesystem setup. When no slab debug root exists it returns without action. Otherwise it creates a child directory named for the cache and installs separate read-only files for allocation-side and free-side object tracking, each bound to the cache with its direction selector.

Debug filesystem contract for slab caches. Directory name equals cache name. Contained files are named alloc_traces and free_traces, each with mode 0400, carrying alloc versus free tracking selectors.

Boot-time sizing table for small allocations. It validates that the minimum allocation size is bounded and a power of two, initializes index entries for sizes below that minimum to the lowest order, and redirects the 96 byte and 192 byte bands to larger orders when alignment minimums of 64 and 128 make the narrow sizes unusable.

Creation of general-purpose allocation caches. It walks every allocation type including reclaim and accounting variants, creates caches for sub-power sizes when the minimum allows plus all power orders across the supported shift range, marks the slab subsystem usable for general allocation, and optionally creates a separate buckets cache that refuses merging.

Per-type cache configuration. Reclaim type requests reclaim accounting, accounting type requests memory accounting unless that facility is disabled in which case it aliases the normal cache, no-extension type requests exclusion from object extensions and merging unless unneeded in which case it aliases normal, and DMA type requests DMA placement. Partition types refuse merging. When accounting is globally enabled, normal caches distinct from reclaim refuse merging while other kinds permit future accounting unless they exclude extensions. Oversized alignment rounds the size up and aliases the requested index to the aligned index, creating the backing cache once.

Need test for extension-free caches. It reports true while allocation profiling can still be enabled, and also when memory accounting is globally enabled while normal and reclaim types share the same index. Otherwise it reports false.

Boot cache creation. Allocation uses non-sleeping context and panics with the cache name on failure. The new descriptor is initialized as a boot cache with the kmalloc marker plus caller flags, linked into the global cache list, and given a reference count of one.

Minimum alignment for general allocation. The effective value is the maximum of the DMA cache alignment requirement, with a bounce-buffer override when that configuration is active and its pool exists, and the architecture slab minimum.

Synchronization of code tag support for object extensions. One build variant compares profiling need against the current static key state and enables or disables the key to match. The alternate build variant is an empty operation.

Randomization of slab freelists at boot. One variant acquires the global slab mutex, initializes a random sequence for every cache on the global list, then releases the mutex. The alternate variant does nothing.

Promotion of a static cache descriptor to a dynamic one. The result is a freshly allocated descriptor carrying the static contents sized by the cache-of-caches object size, with every partial slab and, in debug builds, every full slab on each node repointed to the new descriptor, and with the new descriptor linked globally.

Early setup of sheaf and barn layers for general caches. Capacity is derived from cache geometry with empty arguments, with zero capacity treated as a no-op for tiny or debug configurations. Otherwise per-node barns and per-CPU primary sheaves are allocated. Any allocation failure during this early window panics with the cache name. Aliased caches that already have layers are skipped, and the computed capacity is recorded on success.
Memory initialization reporting levels comprise MMINIT_WARNING, MMINIT_VERIFY and MMINIT_TRACE in that order.

No-operation helpers in early memory initialization. The header guard macro marks inclusion, while CMA pageblock initialization and page flag layout verification are empty operations in this configuration.

Traversal of online nodes and zones. The first online node data accessor and the successor accessor returning null past the last node support iteration. Zone iteration advances within a node and otherwise moves to the first zone of the next online node, yielding null when exhausted.

Zonelist filtering for allocation. Iteration skips entries whose zone index exceeds the allowed maximum, and when a node mask is supplied also skips entries whose zone is absent or whose node is outside the mask. Node membership is always true in non-NUMA builds and follows the zonelist node index otherwise.

Atomic exchange of the last-access CPU field within folio flags. The operation repeatedly reads flags, extracts the prior identifier, replaces the field bits with the new identifier masked to width, and commits with compare and exchange until successful, returning the prior value.
Global per-node data table. A single array indexed by node number holds pointers to node descriptors, sized by the maximum node count.
Fallback address-to-node mapping for builds without populatable tables. Both hot-add and target queries log a one-time notice naming the address and assume node zero.

Emulated NUMA sizing. Minimum fake node size is 32 MiB, with a hash mask clearing lower bits below that size. A global table maps emulated node numbers to physical node numbers, plus a boot-time command line buffer.

CPU attachment for emulated nodes. Adding a CPU resolves its early node and physical node, then sets membership on every online emulated node sharing that physical node. Removing a CPU clears membership on every online node. One build enforces valid online early nodes while the alternate tolerates missing mappings and shares a common helper parameterized by an enable flag.

NUMA topology storage. A count and a row-major square table hold pairwise distances, a mask records parsed nodes, and separate tables describe active versus reserved memory blocks with per-block start, end and node ownership.
Node distance query. In-range pairs return the stored table byte at row-major offset. Out-of-range pairs return LOCAL_DISTANCE when both ends match and REMOTE_DISTANCE otherwise.

Coverage invariant for memory blocks over an interval. When no block overlaps the interval the sentinel NUMA_NO_MEMBLK is reported. Otherwise the overlapping selection ends up sorted by start, with the earliest start at or below the interval start and the latest end at or above the interval end, and with gaps eliminated so each block begins no later than the prior end.

Address-to-node resolution from block tables. A linear scan returns the owning node for the containing block or NUMA_NO_NODE when absent. Target-node queries prefer the active table unless the address is also covered by reserved ranges. Hot-add queries fall back to the first active block when no containing block exists.
Global OOM serialization. Two mutexes exist, one guarding the out-of-memory killer path and one guarding adjustment of victim selection scores.

Out-of-memory constraint names and control knobs. Four constraints are named CONSTRAINT_NONE, CONSTRAINT_CPUSET, CONSTRAINT_MEMORY_POLICY and CONSTRAINT_MEMCG. Controls are named panic_on_oom, oom_kill_allocating_task and oom_dump_tasks, each with mode 0644 using integer vector handlers, with panic bounded between 0 and 2 and dump defaulting to 1.

Out-of-memory reaper state. An atomic counter tracks active victims, a mostly-read flag records whether the killer is disabled, a pointer holds the reaper thread, and a singly linked pending list of tasks is guarded by a dedicated spinlock.

Asynchronous reclamation of victim address spaces. A timer queues the victim unless it already terminated, waking a freezable thread that dequeues one task at a time. Reaping is retried a bounded number of times with idle sleeps when the address space lock is contended. On success or when the space is already marked skipped, the space is hidden from further selection and the queued reference is dropped. Persistent failure logs the victim and dumps lock state.

Reaping traversal within one address space. The space is first marked unstable for user-copy paths, then mappings are visited in reverse order to reduce contention with the exiting owner. Huge and direct-mapping areas are skipped, while anonymous and non-shared file mappings are unmapped for reclamation. The operation reports whether the whole space was covered, and callers skip work when the try-lock fails or the skip marker is already set.

Failure handling across early allocation and topology setup. Boot cache and sheaf allocation failures panic rather than returning errors, overlong alias identifiers yield error pointers, invalid early CPU-to-node associations trigger a fatal check in one build, and folio identifier updates rely on atomic retry loops to avoid lost updates.
Reaper timing and retry bounds plus tracing marker. The tracepoint creation marker is defined, the delay before queuing a victim is 2 times HZ, and the maximum lock retry count is 10.
